title: Question 1
stem:
A child kicks a ball so that it leaves horizontal ground with a velocity of $28 \text{m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $34^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, as shown in Fig. 1.1.
{{figure:figure_1_1}}
Fig. 1.1
Air resistance is negligible. The ball leaves the ground at time $t = 0$.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal component $v_{\mathrm{H}}$ and the vertical component $v_{\mathrm{V}}$ of the velocity of the ball immediately after it has left the ground.
hints: Hint 1: Picture the 28 m s-1 arrow as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with horizontal and vertical sides. Which side is adjacent to the 34 degree angle?
Hint 2: Use cosine for the adjacent (horizontal) side and sine for the opposite (vertical) side, then calculate both to 2 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Resolve the launch velocity into two perpendicular directions**
Any angled velocity can be split into a horizontal part and a vertical part. The horizontal part is adjacent to the angle to the ground, the vertical part is opposite.

Step 2: **Calculate both components**
$$v_H = 28 \cos 34^{\circ} = 23.2 \approx 23 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
$$v_V = 28 \sin 34^{\circ} = 15.7 \approx 16 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
Keep 2 s.f. to match the data. These are the starting values for the rest of the motion.

key_concepts: horizontal and vertical components of projectile velocity

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Show that the ball reaches its maximum height at time $t = 1.6 \text{s}$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what the vertical velocity must be instant by instant at the very top, and what constant acceleration is changing it from your value of $v_V$.
parts.proper_answer: At max height $v = 0$, so $t = v_V/g = 16/9.81 = 1.6 \text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the condition for maximum height**
On the way up gravity slows the ball at $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ downwards. At the very top the ball momentarily stops moving up, so vertical velocity $v = 0$.

Step 2: **Apply $v = u - gt$**
$$0 = v_V - gt$$
$$t = \frac{v_V}{g} = \frac{16}{9.81} \approx 1.63 \approx 1.6 \text{ s}$$
This shows the given time is correct.

markscheme_points.text: horizontal straight line at $v = 23 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 3.2 \text{ s}$

hints: Hint 1: With no air resistance there is no horizontal force, so think about what Newton's first law says about the horizontal speed during the whole 3.2 s flight.
parts.proper_answer: Horizontal straight line at $v = 23 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 3.2 \text{ s}$, labelled H.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise constant $v_H$**
With air resistance negligible, horizontal acceleration is zero. So $v_H$ stays at its initial value of $23 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ all the way from launch to landing.

Step 2: **Sketch line H**
Draw a flat horizontal line at $23 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ on the velocity axis, extending from $t = 0$ to $t = 3.2 \text{ s}$. Label it H.

parts.label: (a)(iv)
parts.text: On Fig. 1.2, sketch the variation of $v_{\mathrm{V}}$ with time $t$ between $t = 0$ and $t = 3.2 \text{s}$. Assume that velocity in the upward direction is positive. Label your line V.

markscheme_points.text: straight diagonal line starting at a positive velocity from $t = 0$ to $t = 3.2 \text{ s}$, crossing the time axis
line starting at $v = 16 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and ending at $v = -16 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

hints: Hint 1: Think about the vertical force acting. With only weight pulling down, how should vertical velocity change with time - steady increase, steady decrease, or curved?
Hint 2: Recall your starting upward speed and think about symmetry: what will the downward speed be when it lands back at ground level after 3.2 s?
Hint 3: Use the time to the top from (a)(ii) to locate where the line must cross zero velocity on the graph.
parts.proper_answer: Straight diagonal line from $v = +16 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 0$ to $v = -16 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 3.2 \text{ s}$, crossing $v = 0$ at $t = 1.6 \text{ s}$, labelled V.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Straight line with constant negative gradient**
Vertical acceleration is constant $-g$ downwards, so the $v_V$-$t$ graph is a straight line sloping downwards. Upward is taken as positive.

Step 2: **Fix the start and end points**
$$\text{at } t = 0, v_V = +16 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
$$\text{at } t = 3.2 \text{ s}, v_V = -16 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
The motion is symmetric, so landing speed downwards equals launch speed upwards.

Step 3: **Fix the zero crossing**
The line crosses $v = 0$ at the top of flight, $t = 1.6 \text{ s}$. Draw the diagonal joining these points and label it V.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: The total change in momentum of the ball between leaving the ground at $t = 0$ and landing on the ground at $t = 3.2 \text{s}$ is $13 \text{kg m s}^{-1}$.
hints: Hint 1: Think of momentum as the quantity of motion - which two properties of a moving object (one to do with matter, one to do with motion) multiply together to give it?
parts.proper_answer: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **State the definition**
Momentum measures how much motion an object carries. It depends on both how much mass is moving and how fast it moves in a given direction:
$$p = mv$$
So momentum = mass x velocity, a vector quantity with unit $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$.

enrichment.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think of momentum as the quantity of motion - which two properties of a moving object (one to do with matter, one to do with motion) multiply together to give it?

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the force that acts on the ball while it is in the air.
hints: Hint 1: Remember force is not just $ma$ here - think of the more general form linking force to how quickly momentum changes while the ball is in the air.
Hint 2: Identify the total momentum change (13 kg m s-1) and the total time in the air (3.2 s), then divide to find the steady force.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use force equals rate of change of momentum**
While in the air the only force is weight, which is constant. Newton's second law in momentum form is:
$$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$

Step 2: **Substitute values**
$$F = \frac{13}{3.2} \approx 4.06 \approx 4.1 \text{ N}$$
This is the weight of the ball acting downwards throughout flight.

enrichment.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: Newton's second law as rate of change of momentum
weight as only force in flight
hints: Hint 1: Remember force is not just $ma$ here - think of the more general form linking force to how quickly momentum changes while the ball is in the air.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Determine the mass of the ball.
hints: Hint 1: You now know the steady force is the weight. Think how weight links to mass, or alternatively how the total change in vertical velocity links to the momentum change.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link force or momentum change to mass**
The force found is the weight $W = mg$. So mass follows directly:
$$m = \frac{F}{g}$$
Equivalently, vertical velocity changes from $+16$ to $-16 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, a change of $32 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, so $\Delta p = m\Delta v$.

Step 2: **Calculate**
$$m = \frac{4.06}{9.81} \approx 0.41 \text{ kg}$$
This is a sensible mass for a football.
